blocks.p: I saw then in my dream that Hopeful looked back and saw Ignorance, whom they had left behind, coming after them.
“Look,” he said to Christian, “how far behind that young man is lagging.”
“Yes, yes, I see him. He doesn’t care for our company.”
“But I don’t think it would have hurt him to keep up with us all this way.”
“That’s true; but I’ll guarantee he thinks otherwise.”
“I think he does. But let’s wait for him anyway.” So they did.
Then Christian said to him, “Come on, man, why are you staying so far behind?”
“I take pleasure in walking alone,” said Ignorance, “a great deal more than in company, unless it’s company I like better.”

Then Christian said to Hopeful, but quietly, “Didn’t I tell you he doesn’t care for our company? Still, come, let’s talk away the time in this lonely place.” Then he turned to Ignorance. “Well, how are you? How do things stand between God and your soul now?”
“I hope well; for I am always full of good impulses that come into my mind to comfort me as I walk.”
“What good impulses? Tell us, please.”
“Why, I think of God and heaven.”
“So do the devils and the damned.”
“But I think of them and desire them.”
“So do many who are never likely to get there. ‘The soul of the sluggard craves, and gets nothing.’” [Prov. 13:4]
“But I think of them, and leave everything for them.”
“That I doubt; for leaving everything is a hard thing, harder than many realize. But why, or by what, are you persuaded that you have left everything for God and heaven?”
“My heart tells me so.”
“The wise man says, ‘Whoever trusts in his own heart is a fool.’” [Prov. 28:26]
“That is said of an evil heart, but mine is a good one.”
“But how do you prove that?”
“It comforts me with hopes of heaven.”
“That may be its deceitfulness; for a man’s heart may comfort him with the hope of something he has no grounds to hope for.”
“But my heart and my life agree, and so my hope is well grounded.”
“Who told you that your heart and your life agree?”
“My heart tells me so.”
“That’s like asking the thief’s partner whether the thief is honest! Your heart tells you so! Unless the Word of God bears witness in this matter, no other testimony is worth anything.”
“But isn’t a heart that has good thoughts a good heart? And isn’t a life lived by God’s commandments a good life?”
“Yes, they are. But it is one thing actually to have these, and quite another only to think you do.”
“Tell me, then, what do you count as good thoughts, and a life lived by God’s commandments?”
“There are good thoughts of different kinds: some about ourselves, some about God, some about Christ, and some about other things.”
“What are good thoughts about ourselves?”
“Those that agree with the Word of God.”
“When do our thoughts about ourselves agree with the Word of God?”

“When we pass the same judgment on ourselves that the Word passes. Let me explain. The Word of God says of people in their natural condition, ‘There is no one righteous; there is no one who does good.’ [Rom. 3] It also says that ‘every intention of the thoughts of man’s heart is only evil continually’ [Gen. 6:5]; and again, ‘The intention of man’s heart is evil from his youth.’ [Gen. 8:21] Now when we think of ourselves this way, and truly feel it, then our thoughts are good ones, because they agree with the Word of God.”
“I will never believe that my heart is as bad as that.”

“Then you have never had one good thought about yourself in your life. But let me go on. The Word passes judgment on our ways as well as on our hearts; and when our thoughts about both agree with its judgment, then they are good.”
“Explain what you mean.”

“Why, the Word of God says that man’s ways are crooked ways, not good but perverse. [Ps. 125:5; Prov. 2:15] It says that by nature people are out of the good way, and have not known it. [Rom. 3] When a man thinks this of his ways, with real feeling and a humbled heart, then his thoughts about his ways are good, because they agree with the judgment of the Word.”
“What are good thoughts about God?”

“Just as with ourselves: when our thoughts of God agree with what the Word teaches of his being and his attributes. But to speak of him in relation to us: we have right thoughts of God when we think that he knows us better than we know ourselves, and can see sin in us when and where we can see none; when we think that he knows our inmost thoughts, and that our heart, with all its depths, is always open to his eyes; and when we think that all our righteousness stinks in his nostrils, and that he cannot bear to see us stand before him in any confidence of our own, even in our best performances.”
“Do you think I am such a fool as to think God can see no further than I can? Or that I would come to God trusting in the best of my performances?”
“Why, then, what do you think in this matter?”
“Why, to be brief, I think I must believe in Christ to be made right with God.”

“What! You think you must believe in Christ, when you don’t see your need of him! You see neither the sin you were born with nor the sins you commit, but have such an opinion of yourself and of what you do that you plainly show you have never seen any need of Christ’s own righteousness to make you right before God. How, then, can you say, ‘I believe in Christ’?”
“I believe well enough, for all that.”
“How do you believe?”

“I believe that Christ died for sinners, and that I shall be freed from the curse and made right before God through his gracious acceptance of my obedience to his law. Or put it this way: Christ, by his merits, makes my religious duties acceptable to his Father, and so I shall be made right.”
“Let me answer this confession of your faith,” said Christian. “First, you believe with an imaginary faith, for this faith is described nowhere in the Word.
“Second, you believe with a false faith, because it takes the power to make you right with God away from Christ’s own righteousness and gives it to yours.
“Third, this faith makes Christ the one who justifies, not your person, but your actions; and your person only for your actions’ sake, which is false.

“Fourth, and therefore, this faith is deceitful, the kind that will leave you under wrath on the day of God Almighty. True saving faith makes the soul, once it sees its condition under the law, run for refuge to Christ’s righteousness. And that righteousness is not some act of grace by which he makes your obedience acceptable to God; it is his own obedience to the law, in doing and suffering for us what the law required of us. That is the righteousness true faith accepts. Wrapped in its folds, and presented by it as spotless before God, the soul is accepted and acquitted of all condemnation.”

“What! Would you have us trust in what Christ did in his own person, apart from us? That idea would loosen the reins on our desires and let us live however we please. For what would it matter how we live, if we can be made right from everything by Christ’s personal righteousness, as long as we believe it?”

“Ignorance is your name,” said Christian, “and as your name is, so are you; this very answer of yours proves it. You are ignorant of what saving righteousness is, and just as ignorant of how to keep your soul, through faith in it, from the heavy wrath of God. Yes, and you are ignorant of the true effect of saving faith in Christ’s righteousness, which is to bow the heart and win it over to God in Christ, to love his name, his Word, his ways, and his people; not what you ignorantly imagine.”
“Ask him,” said Hopeful, “whether Christ has ever been revealed to him from heaven.”
“What! You’re a man for revelations!” said Ignorance. “I believe that what you and all the rest of you say about that is nothing but the product of disordered brains.”
“Why, man!” said Hopeful. “Christ is so hidden in God from the natural understanding of the flesh that no one can know him savingly unless God the Father reveals him.”
“That is your faith, but not mine. Still, I don’t doubt mine is as good as yours, though I don’t have as many fancies in my head as you do.”

“Let me put in a word,” said Christian. “You should not speak so lightly of this matter. For I will boldly say, just as my good companion has, that no one can know Jesus Christ except by the revelation of the Father [Matt. 11:27]; yes, and that faith too, the faith by which the soul takes hold of Christ, if it is the right kind, must be worked in us by the surpassing greatness of his mighty power; and I see, poor Ignorance, that you know nothing of the working of that faith. [1 Cor. 12:3; Eph. 1:18-19] So wake up; see your own wretchedness, and run to the Lord Jesus; and by his righteousness, which is the righteousness of God, for he himself is God, you will be set free from condemnation.”
“You go so fast I can’t keep up with you. Go on ahead; I must stay behind a while.”
Then they said:

blocks.p: Then Christian said to his companion, “Well, come, my good Hopeful, I see that you and I must walk by ourselves again.”
So I saw in my dream that they went on ahead at a good pace, and Ignorance came hobbling after.
“I feel very sorry for this poor man,” said Christian. “It will certainly go badly with him in the end.”

“Alas, there are plenty in our town in his condition,” said Hopeful, “whole families, yes, whole streets, and pilgrims among them too. And if there are so many in our parts, how many do you think there must be in the place where he was born?”

“Indeed the Word says, ‘He has blinded their eyes, so that they cannot see,’ and so on. But now that we are by ourselves, what do you think of such men? Do you think they ever feel convicted of sin, and so have fears that their state is dangerous?”
“No, you answer that question yourself, since you are the older man.”

“Then I say that sometimes, I think, they may. But since they are ignorant by nature, they don’t understand that such convictions are for their good; and so they try desperately to stifle them, and go on presumptuously flattering themselves in the way of their own hearts.”
“I do believe, as you say, that fear does men a great deal of good, and helps set them right when they first begin their pilgrimage.”
“Without any doubt it does, if it is the right kind of fear; for so the Word says: ‘The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.’” [Prov. 1:7; 9:10; Job 28:28; Ps. 111:10]
“How would you describe the right kind of fear?”
“True, or right, fear can be known by three things:
1. by where it comes from: it is caused by saving conviction of sin;
2. it drives the soul to take firm hold of Christ for salvation;

3. it produces and keeps alive in the soul a great reverence for God, his Word, and his ways, keeping the soul tender, and making it afraid to turn from them to the right or to the left, toward anything that might dishonor God, break its peace, grieve the Spirit, or give the enemy cause to speak reproachfully.”
“Well said. I believe you have spoken the truth. Are we almost past the Enchanted Ground now?”
“Why, are you tired of this conversation?”
“No, truly; I only want to know where we are.”

“We have no more than two miles further to go on it. But let’s come back to our subject. The ignorant don’t know that the convictions that make them afraid are for their good, and so they try to stifle them.”
“How do they try to stifle them?”

“First, they think those fears are the devil’s work, though in fact they are God’s; and thinking so, they resist them as things that will ruin them. Second, they think these fears will spoil their faith, when, alas for them, poor men, they have none at all; and so they harden their hearts against them. Third, they assume they ought not to be afraid, and so, in spite of their fears, they grow presumptuously confident. Fourth, they see that these fears would take away their pitiful old homemade holiness, and so they resist them with all their might.”
“I know something of this myself; for before I knew myself, it was this way with me.”
“Well, let’s leave our neighbor Ignorance to himself for now, and take up another profitable question.”
“With all my heart; but you begin again.”
“Well then, about ten years ago, did you know a man named Temporary in your parts, who was keen on religion then?”
“Know him! Yes. He lived in Graceless, a town about two miles from Honesty, and he lived next door to a man called Turnback.”
“Right; in fact he lived under the same roof with him. Well, that man was once deeply awakened. I believe that at that time he had some sight of his sins, and of the wages they had earned.”

“I think so too; for my house was no more than three miles from his, and he often came to see me, and with many tears. I truly pitied the man, and was not altogether without hope for him. But one can see that not everyone who cries ‘Lord, Lord’ enters in.”
“He told me once that he was resolved to go on pilgrimage, as we are doing now. But all of a sudden he struck up an acquaintance with a man called Save-self, and then he became a stranger to me.”
“Since we’re talking about him, let’s look a little into the reasons for the sudden backsliding of men like him.”
“It could be very profitable. But you begin.”
“Well, then, in my judgment there are four reasons for it.

“First, though the consciences of such men are awakened, their minds are not changed. So when the power of guilt wears off, whatever drove them to be religious is gone, and they naturally go back to their old course. They are like a dog sick from what it has eaten: while the sickness lasts, it vomits everything up, not by choice, if a dog can be said to choose, but because its stomach is troubled; once the sickness passes, since it has no real distaste for its vomit, it turns around and licks it all up, just as it is written, ‘The dog returns to its own vomit.’ [2 Pet. 2:22] These men are hot for heaven only because they feel and fear the torments of hell; and as that fear cools, their desire for heaven cools with it, until, when their guilt and fear are gone, it dies, and they return to their old course.

“Second, they are ruled by slavish fear; I mean the fear of men, for ‘the fear of man lays a snare.’ [Prov. 29:25] As long as the flames of hell are around their ears, they seem hot for heaven; but when that terror has passed a little, they have second thoughts: that it is only sensible not to risk losing everything, for they know not what, or at least not to bring needless trouble on themselves. And so they fall in with the world again.

“Third, the shame that goes along with religion lies like a stone in their path. They are proud and haughty, and in their eyes religion is low and contemptible. So when they have lost their sense of hell and the wrath to come, they go back to their former course.

“Fourth, guilt and the thought of terror are painful to them. They don’t like to see their misery before they come into it, though seeing it first, if they were willing to look, might make them run where the righteous run and are safe. So once they are rid of their awakenings to the terrors and wrath of God, they gladly harden their hearts, and choose the ways that will harden them more and more.”

“You are pretty close to the heart of it,” said Christian, “for at the bottom of it all is the lack of any change in their mind and will. They are just like the criminal standing before the judge: he shakes and trembles and seems to repent with all his heart, but at the bottom of it all is the fear of the noose, not any hatred of the crime. Set him free, and he will be a thief and a rogue still; whereas if his mind were changed, he would be different.”
“Now that I have shown you the reasons they go back, you show me how they go about it.”
“I will, gladly.
1. They turn their thoughts away, as much as they can, from remembering God, death, and the judgment to come.
2. Then, little by little, they give up private duties: prayer alone, restraining their desires, watchfulness, sorrow for sin, and the like.
3. Then they avoid the company of lively and warm-hearted Christians.
4. After that they grow cold toward public duties: hearing the Word, reading, godly conversation, and the like.
5. Then they begin, as we say, to pick holes in the coats of some of the godly, and devilishly, so that some weakness they have spotted gives them an excuse to throw religion behind their backs.
6. Then they attach themselves to worldly, loose, and immoral men, and keep company with them.
7. Then they give way to worldly and indecent talk in secret, glad if they can find the same in anyone counted honest, so that they can do it more boldly on that example.
8. After this they begin to play with little sins openly.

9. And then, hardened, they show themselves for what they are. And so, launched again into the gulf of misery, unless a miracle of grace prevents it, they perish forever in their own self-deceptions.”
